retail.label: Retail
retail.description: Online stores and delivery services — where to go when an order, refund, or delivery goes sideways.
retail.intro: Retail customer service almost always comes down to the same few problems: an order that hasn't arrived, arrived damaged, or a refund that hasn't shown up yet. Every retailer below handles these through its own official channels — a help center, live chat, and in some cases a published phone line — and processing times vary by company and by how the order was paid for. Before you reach out, have your order number and the email address used at checkout ready; most retailers ask for both to look up a purchase. If a company here doesn't list a phone number, that's because it isn't published on their official site, not something we missed — use the verified chat link instead. Every listing links to that retailer's own support page, so you can confirm the same information yourself.

social.label: Social Media
social.description: Social platforms — most don't offer phone support, so knowing the real help channel matters even more.
social.intro: Social platforms almost never offer a phone line. Support runs through in-app reporting, a help center, or in Meta's case an AI assistant, and that's deliberate on the platform's part, not a gap in our research. That also makes account-recovery scams especially common here: if you're locked out or think your account was hacked, be wary of any site or ad promising a phone number to call, since none of the platforms below publish one. The safest path is always the official help center link on each page, verified to go to that company's own domain. Common reasons people look these companies up include a compromised account, a forgotten password, a suspended account, or reporting impersonation — each help center below has a dedicated flow for exactly that.

email.label: Email Providers
email.description: Email and account providers — for lockouts, hacked accounts, and recovery.
email.intro: Email providers, like social platforms, rarely offer phone support for personal accounts — Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo Mail all route account issues through self-service help articles or, in Microsoft's case, a sign-in-gated chat option. The most common reason people search for these providers is being locked out or suspecting their account was compromised, which is unfortunately the exact scenario scammers exploit with fake account-recovery phone numbers. None of the providers listed here publish a general support line, so treat any number claiming otherwise as unverified. Each listing links directly to that provider's own help center, where you can start password recovery or report suspicious activity through their real, official flow.

streaming.label: Streaming
streaming.description: Video and music subscriptions — billing issues, playback problems, and canceling a plan.
streaming.intro: Streaming support issues are usually about billing or access — a payment that didn't go through, a plan you want to change, or trouble signing in on a new device. None of the services listed here publish a general customer service phone number; support runs through their help center and, once you're signed in, a chat option tied to your account. That's standard across the industry, not a gap in our listings. Before contacting any of them, have the email address tied to your subscription ready, since most support flows start by confirming your account. Each listing below links directly to that service's own official help center, checked against the source and dated.

telecom.label: Telecom
telecom.description: Phone and internet carriers — for billing, outages, device, and account issues.
telecom.intro: Telecom support covers more ground than most categories here — billing questions, outages, device and SIM issues, and account changes all route through the same customer service lines. Unlike social media or streaming, telecom carriers do publish real phone numbers, and we've verified each one directly against the carrier's own site, along with its stated hours. Carriers often run separate lines for different issues — new service versus an existing account versus technical support — so check the full listing below rather than just the headline number if your issue is more specific. As always, treat any number you find elsewhere, like a search ad or forum post, as unverified until you confirm it here or on the carrier's own site.

shipping.label: Shipping Carriers
shipping.description: Package carriers — for tracking, delays, and claims on a shipment that's gone missing.
shipping.intro: Shipping and carrier support almost always comes down to one question: where is my package, and why hasn't it moved. UPS, FedEx, and USPS each publish real phone numbers and automated tracking tools, verified directly against their own sites below. Before you contact any of them, have the tracking number ready — it's the fastest way to get a real answer, often faster than a phone call. If a package shows “delivered” but isn't there, most carriers ask you to wait a short window before filing a claim, since GPS-marked deliveries are occasionally logged a little early. For lost, damaged, or stolen packages, you'll typically need the tracking number and, for higher-value items, proof of contents or purchase. As with every category here, treat any “carrier support” number you find outside this page as unverified until you confirm it against the carrier's own site.

airlines.label: Airlines
airlines.description: Major US airlines — for booking changes, delays, cancellations, and baggage issues.
airlines.intro: Airline customer service tends to split into two very different situations: a routine question (baggage, seat changes, mileage) and a disrupted trip (delay, cancellation, misconnection) where minutes matter. Delta, American, United, and Southwest all publish real phone numbers, and we've verified each one directly against the airline's own site, along with its stated hours. If your flight is disrupted, the airline's app or website often rebooks you faster than waiting on hold — check there first. For anything involving a refund or compensation claim, keep your confirmation number and boarding pass on hand; airlines ask for both before they can look up a reservation. As always, be wary of any “airline support” number you find in a search ad or forum post that isn't listed on the airline's own official site.

rideshare.label: Ride-Hailing & Delivery
rideshare.description: Ride-hailing and delivery apps — for trip issues, missing items, and safety concerns.
rideshare.intro: Uber, Lyft, and Instacart handle support almost entirely in-app rather than by phone — a fare dispute, a missing delivery item, or a driver issue is usually resolved fastest through the trip or order itself, not a general support line. We've verified each company's actual phone and chat situation directly against their own site below, including where a published number exists versus where support is app-only. Have your trip or order ID ready before reaching out; it's the first thing these companies ask for, since it ties the issue to a specific driver, shopper, or delivery. For anything involving a safety concern, use the in-app emergency or safety reporting tool first — it routes to a dedicated team faster than general support. Treat any “Uber support number” or similar found outside the app or the company's own site as unverified.

insurance.label: Insurance
insurance.description: Auto and home insurers — for policy questions, billing, and filing a claim.
insurance.intro: Insurance support covers a wide range — a routine policy change, a billing question, and an active claim after an accident or loss are all handled differently, and timing matters most for the last one. GEICO, Progressive, State Farm, and Allstate each publish real phone numbers, verified directly against their own sites below, often with a separate line specifically for filing or checking a claim versus general policy service. Have your policy number ready before calling; most insurers ask for it immediately to pull up your account. If you're filing a claim after an accident, photos, a police report (if one was filed), and the other party's information will speed things up considerably. This is a category scammers specifically target after accidents and natural disasters — treat any “claims number” you find outside the insurer's own official site as unverified until you confirm it here or directly with them.
